source_title: Expansionary policy may not help amid global inflation: Ashok Lahiri - Business Standard
source_excerpt: With global inflation showing signs of firming, particularly in food and petroleum products, and the threat of El Niño adding to price pressures, a knee-jerk expansionary policy response may not be appropriate, said NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Lahiri on Friday. Lahiri favoured a cautious approach while responding to a question from the media, on whether monetary tightening could lead to a slowdown in economic activity and whether there was a need to step up efforts to boost private capital investment. He was speaking on the sidelines of the CII Banking Colloquium here. Earlier this month, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Reserve Bank of India unanimously voted to raise the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 per cent. Interacting with mediapersons, Lahiri said the world was facing uncertainty, pointing to the Strait of Hormuz and the uncertainty over when it would reopen. “If you are implying whether the government in such a situation should have an expansionary policy, the MPC has increased the rate…. I think it’s better to be safe than sorry,” he said. He added that inflation across the world was showing signs of “slightly stiffening”, particularly in food and petroleum products. “And El Niño is also creating some concerns. So in such a situation, I don’t think a knee-jerk expansionary thing is very useful.”Earlier in the day, speaking on ‘Banking Beyond Credit: Powering Eastern India’s Industrial Growth’ at the CII event, Lahiri said banks could act as matchmakers, benefiting both the state and themselves by tapping investment opportunities. “Going beyond credit, what can banks do to improve the situation? First, banks have contact not only with entrepreneurs and prospective investors across the country, but also extensive knowledge of business opportunities in the state and of the state government. They can act as matchmakers, benefiting the state as well as investors, while benefiting themselves from the business opportunity of funding a part of the investment through credit,” he said. He also pointed to regional variations in the credit-deposit (CD) ratio, which stood at 93.6 per cent in the southern region in 2023, while the eastern region recorded the lowest ratio at 47.5 per cent. In the eastern region, the five states of Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Sikkim and West Bengal, along with the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, had CD ratios ranging from 32.6 per cent to 51.1 per cent. Lahiri said West Bengal had missed out on technological improvements brought about by successive industrial revolutions. “We need to make amends. We need to leapfrog and catch up with the most efficient producers of the world. That will automatically generate investment, income, demands of pay, an increase in credit flows from banks,” he said. He called for launching a couple of marquee projects to “announce the start of a new epoch of growth in West Bengal”. “The setting up of a state-of-the-art, deep sea port, and the launch of a modern industrial park in Singur provide those examples. In a state, where aspirations have collapsed because of the decades-long relative decay, such projects would serve as a wake-up call to investors, businessmen, bankers, as well as this general public,” he said. He also called for inviting and facilitating the setting up of a few new large-scale industrial units. Banks find it cheaper and administratively more convenient to lend to one large unit than to hundreds of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), the NITI Aayog vice-chairman pointed out. However, banks also have a major role to play in this journey, Lahiri said, adding that there was much to be done in microfinance, where West Bengal is a leading player. “It is important to remember that the industrial stalwarts of today, like the Birlas and Ambanis, also began as small enterprises. Banks have a role to play in nurturing the MSMEs of today who are going to be big guns of tomorrow,” he added.
